newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin comes clean on health after many denials.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin comes clean on health after many denials.

text.p: There was something strangely repetitive about the Kremlin's fierce denials that Russian President Boris Yeltsin was ill, rather than simply tired.
The president looked distant and wooden in rare television appearances, speaking slowly and holding one arm stiffly by his side. He disappeared for days on end.
Newspapers speculated that he needed an operation, but aides dismissed every report. The president was in a "brisk mood", was "working on documents", was "in full control", they said.
But Yeltsin himself came clean about his health on Thursday. In an unprecedented admission for a Russian leader, he announced he will have a heart operation this month.
"I want to have a society based on truth here, that means no longer hiding what we used to hide," he said in an interview shown on NTV commercial television.
"I have undergone routine checks and during these checks they have found something wrong with my heart. The recomendations of doctors, our doctors, were for an operation or to work in a passive way."
But passive work is out of character for Yeltsin, a workaholic who has taken pride in his ability to stay at his desk or tour the country for 16 or 20 hours a day.
He charged like a madman through Russia's presidential election campaign this spring, travelling frequently in a hectic U.S.-style meet-the-people campaign.
The action came to an abrupt halt on June 26, when the president cancelled meetings, disappeared and finally, after over two months of official equivocation, admitted he was ill.
He is currently on holiday outside Moscow and is getting ready to meet German Chancellor Helmut Kohl at the weekend.
The rare television interview came one day after Yeltsin's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais promised changes in information policy to stop the Russian rumour mill.
"There is a huge amount of speculation, justified to a certain extent," Chubais told a news conference.
"We have to make serious changes in the information policy of the administration. We must understand that the less official information there is, the more speculation and rumours."
But the new openness has not yet extended to any details about what sort of operation the president, 65, will undergo.
Yeltsin had two heart attacks last year, caused by ischaemia -- which reduces blood supply to the heart.
A Kremlin source told Reuters the operation was likely to be bypass surgery, in which clogged arteries are replaced to improve the blood supply to the heart.
Cardiologists said this had become a fairly routine operation in Western countries.

"There are standard methods that have been used for cardiac bypass surgery, techniques which have been standardised in the last 10 or 20 years," said Robert Kormos, an associate professor at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center.
"Generally in the U.S. most patients go home after four or five days and there is a two to four week recovery period."
